2. While scrutinizing these Orders, the Committee noted in some cases
considerable time lag between issue of notifications and their laying. The
annexed statement also indicates the period of delay in cases where notifications
have not been laid as per the schedule prescribed by the Committee. The
Committee observed that out of total 321 delayed notifications there were 185
notifications where no delay statement was appended. However, the bulk of
delayed notifications were from Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
which cames around 79.75% of total delayed notifications.
The observations/recommendations of the Committee in respect of the
specific Ministries/Departments where delay in laying of Notifications has been
noticed are as follows: -
(i) Ministry of Agriculture
(Department of Agriculture and Cooperation and Department of Animal
Husbandry Dairying and Fisheries)
Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture and Cooperation)
have laid 18 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 1 to 18) out of which 2 notifications (Sl.
Nos. 1 and 16) have been delayed by 3 and 9 months respectively. There was
no delay statement attached with one notification (Sl. No. 1) which was delayed
by 3 months. Another notification (Sl. No. 16) was delayed by 9 months but
Ministry has appended delay statement indicating the reason of the delay.
Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Animal Husbandry Dairying and
Fisheries) have laid 4 notifications (Sl. Nos. 19 to 22) All of these were delayed
by 5 months to 46 months and accompanied with delay statements. The reasons
of delay given therein are as under:-
“As per consolidated guidelines of framing/amendment/relaxation of
Recruitment Rules issued by DoPT OM No. AB.14017/48/2010-
Estt.(RR) dated 31.12.2010, para 5.3 of Part-V stipulates that “Although
the Recruitment Rules are statutory in nature, the copies of the notification
of the same need not be placed on the Table of both the Houses of

6
Parliament as Article 309 of the Constitution, under which these are
framed, does not prescribe this being done”. The Coconut Development
Board (Group ‘C’ post) Recruitment Regulations, 2012 have been framed
as per above mentioned guidelines of DoPT. Hence, it was not laid on
the Table of both the Houses of Parliament. The delay may kindly be
condoned.”
The Committee is unable to accept the reason given by the Ministry
for delay in laying of notifications despite the recommendations of the
Committee in this regard in its 82nd Report (para 4.31) which clearly
says that “... There is no reason why the Rules made under Article 309 of
the Constitution should not be laid before Parliament. There have been
some cases where the Rules made under Article 309 of the Constitution have
been laid before the Parliament. The Committee, therefore, strongly feels
and recommends that in order to maintain a uniform practice all the rules
made under delegated authority whether under various act of Parliament or
Article 309 of the Constitution should be laid before the Parliament. In
case, however, Government feels that the non-existence of the laying provision
in Article 309 is the reason for not laying the Rules made thereunder, the
Committee recommends that Article 309 of the Constitution be suitably
amended, so as to ensure that all the Rules made thereunder are laid before
the Parliament.” The Committee also takes note of the inordinate delay
of approximately 46 months in laying Rules which is not just acceptable
to the Committee and it recommends that Ministry of Agriculture should
in future strictly adhere to the laying procedure and whenever a delay
occurs, the Parliament is kept informed of the reason for the same by
appending a delay statement. The Committee hopes that Ministry would
strive to lay the notifications on the Table of the House at the first earliest
opportunity available.
(ii) Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
(Department of Pharmaceuticals)
Only one notification that the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers

7
(Department of Pharmaceuticals) (Sl. No. 23) have laid was delayed by 5
months and no delay statement appended thereto. The Committee is not
happy over the delay in laying of the only notification by the Ministry of
Chemicals and Fertilizers (Department of Pharmaceuticals) by 5 months.
Further there is no delay statement appended to that giving reason as to
what caused such delay. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the
Ministry to take care that such instances of delay do not recur in future
and in case of any delay in laying, a delay statement should invariably be
appended.
(iii) Ministry of Civil Aviation
Ministry of Civil Aviation have laid only three Notifications (Sl. Nos. 24
to 26) on the Table of the House during the Session. There has been delay of 7
months each in case of Sl. No. 24 and 25 and delay of 6 months in case of Sl.
No. 26. The Ministry has attached delay statement with each of these delayed
notifications and cited administrative reasons for not laying the notifications in
time.
The Committee hopes that the Ministry would avoid such instances
of delay in laying of subordinate legislation in future and would remove
lacuna, if any, administrative or any other causing delay. The Committee
also impresses upon the Ministry to take note of the fact that in case
there is a delay in the laying of any Statutory Notifications, the same
should be accompanied by a delay statement while it is being laid . The
Committee also advises the Ministry of Civil Aviation to avoid recurrence
of delays due to administrative reasons in future.
(iv) Ministry of Communication and Information Technology
(Department of Information Technology and Department of Posts)
Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (Department
of Information Technology) have laid 2 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 37-38) and out
of these notification one was delayed by 6 months with no delay statement

8
attached to it. The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology
(Department of Posts) have laid only one Notification (Sl. No. 39) which was
delayed by 5 months. The Notification was attached with delay statement. The
reasons of delay given by the Ministry is as under:-
“The copies of the Gazette Notification which was published in the Gazette
of India Extraordinary, Part II – Section 3 – sub Section (i) vide No. 497
[GSR 734 (E)] dated October 01, 2012 regarding revision of Speed Post
tariff could not be laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha during the winter
Session of Parliament due to the paucity of time. The notification is now
being laid on the Table of Rajya Sabya during the Budget Session of
Parliament”
The Committee noted with serious concern that Ministry of
Communication and Information Technology (Department of
Information Technology and Department of Posts) have failed to lay the
notifications in time on the Table of the House due to paucity of time.
The laying of notifications on the Table of the House is a statutory
obligation which should be fulfilled without delay. However, the Ministry
have shown lukewarm approach towards their duty toward Parliament.
The Committee recommends that Ministry of Communication and
Information Technology should adhere strictly to the schedule as
recommended by the Committee in its 131
st Report for timely laying of
Subordinate Legislation. The Committee hope that Ministry would avoid
citing such unworthy reasons for delay in future.
(v) Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Ministry of Corporate Affairs have laid 20 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 51 to
70). Out of these 10 Notifications have been delayed by 3 to 5 months. Only
one delayed Notification (Sl. No. 52) was attached with delay statement and
other nine Notifications (Sl. Nos. 53 to 61) did not have any delay statement
citing the exact reasons for delay. The Ministry has stated the following reasons
of delay in regard to G.S.R. 736 (E):-

9
“The notification relating to the GSR No. 736 (E) dated 01.10.2012 on
Amendment in Rule 10(i) of Companies (Issue of Indian Depository
Receipt) Rules, 2004 was sent to Government Press for printing on
01.10.2012. The said notification could not be laid before both the Houses
of Parliament during winter session of the Parliament, 2012 due to delay
in receiving the Gazette copy of the notification by this Ministry and
when it was collected, the session was over on 19.12.2012 (Rajya Sabha)
and 20.12.2012 (Lok Sabha). Hence the said notification got delayed.”
The Committee regrets to note that Ministry of Corporate Affairs
have delayed laying of a number of notifications, many of which do not
have delay statement attached to them. The Committee invites attention
to its recommendations contained in its 135th Report that in case of
delay in laying of notifications, delay statement should invariably be
accompanied with them. As for reason of delay tendered by Ministry for
one notification (Sl. No. 52) stating that delay was caused due to late
receipt of printed copies of notifications, the Committee would like to
impress upon the Ministry of Corporate Affairs to evolve suitable
mechanism to eliminate such instances of delay in future particularly
on account of delay in receiving printed copies of the notifications. The
Committee further recommends that the Ministry should take note of
the time schedule as prescribed by it for laying of Subordinate Legislation
and take necessary corrective steps so that such instances do not recur.
(vi) Ministry of Defence
The Ministry of Defence have laid 4 Notifications and out of which two
were delayed by 3 to 8 months. One of the Notification had delay statement
attached to it whereas another did not have any delay statement with it. The
reasons for delay given by the Ministry are as under:-
“The Jalandhar Cantonment Octroi (Amendment) Bye-laws, 2012 were
issued on 12.06.2012 from the file of Jalandhar Cantonment Board under
the signature of its Chief Executive Officer (CEO). As such the File was

10
returned to Jalandhar Cantonment Board through DGDE on 13.06.2012,
but the published copy of the Notification could be received in the Ministry
only on 4.2.2013. As such, the Notification could not be laid during
Winter Session of Parliament, 2012.
The delay in laying of papers on the Table of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha is
due to delay in getting published copies of the Notification. It is requested
that the marginal delay on the part of Ministry of Defence may kindly be
condoned.”
The Committee finds that laying of notifications was delayed due
to late receipt of printed copies of notifications in the Ministry. In this
context the Committee observes that it is Ministry’s responsibility to
ensure that Subordinate Legislation is laid before the Parliament within
the prescribed schedule and accordingly, it is for the Ministry only to
ensure that they receive the same timely from the statutory bodies under
them. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Defence may
take necessary remedial measures to ensure that papers are received
timely in the Ministry from the statutory bodies.
(vii) Ministry of Environment and Forests
Ministry of Environment and Forests have laid 5 Notifications (Sl. Nos.
75 to 79) during the Session. Out of these, three Notifications (Sl. Nos. 75 –
76 and 78) were delayed by 4 months to 6 months and moreover no delay
statement was appended to any of three delayed notifications.
The Committee notes that three of its notifications which were not
only delayed by four to six months also did not have any delay statement
attached to them. The Committee views it seriously and reiterate its
recommendations (contained in its 135th Report) that in case there is
delay in laying of Statutory Orders, the concerned Ministry/Department
should invariably append a delay statement. The Committee further
impresses the Ministry that it is their obligation towards the Parliament

11
to invariably apprise it about the reasons for delay through delay
statement in case they are unable to lay any Subordinate Legislation on
time.
(viii) Ministry of Finance
(Department of Financial Services)
Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) have laid 31
Notifications (Sl. Nos. 101 to 131). Out of these 9 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 111,
116 – 122 and 131) were delayed. The delay period ranges from 10 months to
31 months. The Ministry had attached delay statement with 8 notifications
whereas no statement was attached/appended with one notification. The reasons
for delay given by the Ministry is as under:-
“The Copies of the Gazettee Notifications could not be laid on the Table
of the Rajya Sabha as printed copies of the same were not received from
Regional Rural Banks in time. The delay has occurred as the Regional
Rural Banks which are spread out all over the country have to send the
Regulations to Government Press, New Delhi for publication. Thereafter,
these are sent back to the concerned Regional Rural Banks which then
sent it to the Ministry. The delay is thus in the administrative procedure/
process.”
The Committee does not accept the reasons of delay given by the
Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) and expresses
its serious concern over such inordinate delay which ranges from 10
months to 31 months. The Committee wonders that how can
administrative procedural process take 10 to 31 months to receive
Notifications and complete procedural formalities. The Committee feels
that Ministry did not take adequate precaution to avoid the delay and
made no serious efforts to lay the Notifications in time which is in
contravention of its statutory obligation to Parliament. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry must take appropriate step to remove
lacuna, if any, administrative or any other, causing such long delay and

12
wish it would strive to keep delay to the minimum by playing a more
proactive role and pursuing concerned organisations to act with
promptness in future.
(ix) Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
(Department of Health and Department of AYUSH)
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (Department of Health) have
laid 7 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 228 to 234). Only one Notification was delayed
by 8 months. However, no delay statement was enclosed with it.
Department of AYUSH have also laid 5 Notifications and one Notification
was delayed by 3 months and laid with delay statement attached to it. The
reasons given by the Ministry are as follows:-
“Laying of Gazette Notification of amendment made in Rule 161 of the
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 vide GSR No. 844 (E) dated 16.11.2012
regarding “insertion of botanical names of plants based ingredients along
with plant part(s) and form of ingredients to be mentioned on label”
published by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare was to be laid in
both Houses of Parliament. However due to the fact that in the final
notification some typographical error was observed and it had to be
rectified as per the prescribed procedure, hence, the notification could
not be laid within the stipulated time period. After rectification of the
error, now the notification is being submitted along with amended version
GSR No. 105 (E) dated 19.02.2013 before both the Houseds of Parliament.”
The Committee have noted the reason cited by the Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare that due to typographical error, the
notification could not be laid in time. The reasons given by the Ministry
seems to be justified and well taken. The Ministry should in future take
care that such instances do not recur and that notification were laid
within the time schedule prescribed by the Committee. The Committee,
therefore, impresses upon the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to

13
be watchful so that such error do not occur and consequential delay is
avoided in future. The Committee also emphasises that in case of delay
in laying of notifications, Ministry should append delay statement with
the notifications.
(x) Ministry of Home Affairs
The Ministry of Home Affairs have laid 21 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 240 -
260) during the Session. Out of total Notifications laid 14 Notifications have
been delayed. Out of these 12 Notifications have average delay period of 5
months whereas one Notification (Sl. No 240) was delayed by 4 months and
no delay statement was appended to 13 notifications. One Notification (Sl. No.
242) was delayed by 12 months and also had delay statement appended to it.
The reasons given by the Ministry are as follows:-
“Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant-in-Aid to Panchayati Raj Institutions)
(Amendment) Rules, 2012 was published in the Andaman & Nicobar
Gazette (Extraordinary) vide notification No. 08 dated 20/01/2012. As
per laid down procedure, the said Rules should have been laid as soon as
may be after it is made before each House of Parliament while it is in
session for a total period of 30 days. It could not be laid before both the
Houses of Parliament in time for want of certain clarifications from UT
of Andaman & Nicobar Administration. Clarifications sought from the
Andaman & Nicobar Administration have now been received.
The delay is regretted. These Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant-in-Aid
to Panchayati Raj Institutions) (Amendment) Rules, 2012 are now being
laid in both the Houses of Parliament in current session.”
The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the large proportion
of Notifications, which comes around 67% of total notifications, being
delayed by the Ministry. The Committee further takes serious note of
the fact that the Ministry in majority of cases did not even bother to
provide the reasons for such delayed laying of Notifications. In absence

14
of any delay statement with any of the delayed notifications, Committee
finds it difficult to ascertain causes of delay. The Committee invites
attention to the recommendations made in its 135th Report wherein it is
laid down that it is essential to append a delay statement in case of delay
in laying of statutory orders. The committee, therefore, impresses upon
the Ministry of Home Affairs to strictly adhere to the time schedule in
laying of Notifications and should invariably append delay statement in
each case of delayed notifications .
(xi) Ministry of Human Resource Development
(Department of Higher Education)
The Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Higher
Education) have laid 7 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 261 to 267). Out of which 3
notifications were delayed by 4 to 5 months. All the delayed notifications were
appended with delay statement. The reasons given by the Ministry is that it
took some time to complete the procedural formalities and therefore, papers
could not be laid in time.
The Committee is not convinced of the vague reasons of delay
given by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of
Higher Education) that due to time taken to complete procedural
formalities, the Ministry could not lay the notifications in time. If, it
was so, the Ministry should have foreseen the things beforehand and
would have acted promptly. The Committee castigates this lackadaisical
approach by the Ministry and advises them to take care in future in
laying of notifications so that delay could be avoided.
(xii) Ministry of Law and Justice
(Department of Justice & Department of Legal Affairs)
Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Justice) have laid one
Notification (Sl. No. 280) on the Table of the House with a delay period of one
year and five months without any delay statement appended to it. Department

15
of Legal Affairs have laid 4 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 281 to 284). All the 4
notifications were delayed and delay ranges from 8 months to 17 months.
However, all the Notifications laid by Department of Legal Affairs were appended
with delay statement. The reasons of delay given by the Department is that due
to voluminous work throughout the year, work relating to laying of notifications
could not be done in time inadvertently.
The Committee accepts that Ministry of Law and Justice is laden
with voluminous work and it may happen that the work may remain
undone inadvertently. However, the Committee impress upon the
Ministry that it is their statutory obligation to lay the notifications in
time on the Table of the House. Therefore Committee hopes that Ministry
would strive to adhere to laying schedule and avoid recurrence of such
delays in future.
(xiii) Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (Department
of Personnel and Training)
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (Department of
Personnel and Training) have laid 10 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 285 to 294). Two
of these Notifications were delayed and the delay period was 5 months and 3
month each. The delay statement was appended with one of these Notifications.
The reasons of delay is given as under:-
“A copy of the Notification could be obtained only on 26.12.2012.
However, by the date the Winter Session of the Parliament was over.”
The Committee is not convinced of the reason given by the Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions that notification was
received on 26.12.2012 and by then Parliament’s winter Session was
already over. The Committee advises the Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions to be more vigilant in future so that such delay
could be avoided.

16
(xiv) Ministry of Railways
Ministry of Railways have laid 4 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 298 to 301).
Only one of them (Sl. No. 300) was delayed by 3 months and accompanied
with delay statement. The reasons given by the Ministry for delay is as under:-
“The Indian Railways (Penalties for activities affecting cleanliness at
railway premises) Rules, 2012 G .S.R. 846 (E) published in the Gazette
of India Extraordinary Part-II Section 3 Sub-section-I could not be laid
down on the Table of the House due to an inadvertent oversight. The
same is therefore laid on the Table of the House.”
The Committee recommends that such instances should not be
repeated in future. Ministry of Railways must endeavour to lay the
notifications on the Table of House with upmost promptness.
(xv) Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways have laid highest number
of notification during the Session which come around 374 Notifications (Sl.
Nos. 302-675). Out of these 256 Notifications have been delayed. The Ministry
did not append any delay statement with 105 delayed notifications (Sl. Nos.
306–310, 313–326, 334–347, 355–56, 358, 362–369, 401–403, 407–410, 413–
414. 416–431, 434–451, 455–458, 461–463, 465–468, 472–474, 476 & 478–
479). However, 151 delayed notifications were appended with delay statements.
The delay period ranges from 3 months to 19 months. The reason of delay
given by the Ministry is that it took some time to collect the papers and complete
the procedural formalities therefore, papers could not be laid in time on the
Table of both Houses of Parliament.
The Committee does not accept the reasons of the delay given by
the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways that it took some time to
collect the papers and complete the procedural formalities. The
Committee wonders how can it take one year to receive Notifications
and to complete procedural formalities. The Committee feels that Ministry

17
did not take adequate precaution to avoid the delay. The Committee
further takes a serious view of the fact that even after delay of one year
in certain case Ministry did not feel it necessary to append a delay
statement so as to apprise the Parliament of the reasons of delay in
laying of Notifications on the Table of the House. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should initiate urgent measures so as to
avoid delay in completing the procedural formalities so that such delay
can be eliminated.
(xvi) Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
(Department of Social Justice and Empowerment)
The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Department of Social
Justice and Empowerment) have laid only one Notifications (Sl. No. 676)
which was delayed by 22 months and moreover Ministry did not even bother
to append a delay statement citing the reasons for such extraordinary delay on
their part.
The Committee is not happy that the only notification that Ministry
of Social Justice and Empowerment have laid, has been extraordinary
delayed. Further, there is no reason given for this delay. This is in
contravention of Committee’s recommendation given in its 135 Report
that Notification which are delayed should invariably be accompanied by
delay statement. The Committee would like the Ministry of Social Justice
and Empowerment to take necessary steps to obviate such delay and in
case of delay in laying of Notifications, delay statement should invariably
be accompanied with them.
(xvii) Ministry of Urban Development
Ministry of Urban Development have laid one Notifications (Sl. No. 683)
during the Session which was delayed by 8 months. The reasons given by the
Ministry for delay is as under:-
“Copies of the Annual Report and Annual Accounts of Delhi Urban Art

18
Commission (DUAC) for the year 2011-12 and Delhi Urban Art Commission
(Secretary) Recruitment Rules, 2012 which were required to be laid on the
Table of Rajya Sabha in the Winter Session of 2012 were sent to Rajya Sabha
Secretariat on 17.12.2012. However, these were returned by the Secretariat
citing shortage of time. Therefore, the same are being laid on the Table of
Rajya Sabha during the Budget Session, 2013.
Delay caused in laying the above documents on the Table of the Rajya
Sabha is regretted.”
The Committee is not convinced with the reasons given by the
Ministry of Urban Development that notification could not be laid in
time due to curtailment of the Winter Session of 2012. Committee
impresses upon the Ministry of Urban Development to endeavour to lay
the notification at the first available opportunity on the Table of the
House so as to fulfill statutory obligation.
Before the commencement of each Session of Parliament Ministries
are informed about the dates of sitting of House and dates allotted to
each Ministries. In case of laying of notifications, Ministries are informed
to bring the notifications to Committee Section 3 working days before
the day/date of laying so that laying process can be completed. But the
Ministries do not adhere to the time schedule and bring the copies for
laying at the fag end of the Session. This causes a great inconvenience
to the Secretariat. The Ministry of Urban Development is advised to
stick to the time schedule to avoid such situation.
The Committee, time and again have emphasized that laying or
rules/regulations/orders is a statutory obligation and should be completed
on priority basis within specified time-frame. The Ministry of Urban
Development should understand the implication of such failures. However,
the Ministry of Urban Development has not complied with the
recommendations of the Committee in this regard. The Committee once

19
again emphasizes that Ministry of Urban Development should adhere to
the time schedule in laying of notifications as prescribed in Committee’s
131st Report.
3. Committee impresses upon all the Ministries/Departments to take
immediate steps to ensure timely and proper laying of subordinate legislation.
The Committee, accordingly, wishes to bring to the notice of all Ministries/
Departments of the Government of India, particularly, the defaulting ones, the
following recommendations, as contained in its 131st, 135th, 152nd , 192nd
and 201st Reports:
“Orders required to be laid before the House should be laid (i) if
the House is not in Session, during the Session immediately following
the date of publication of the Order in the Official Gazette and (ii) if the
House is in Session, on the date of the publication of the Order, during
its continuance and in case the time lag between the date of publication
and the date of the closing of the Session is less than 15 clear days,
before the expiry of the Session immediately following the said Session.
All the Ministries/Departments of Government of India should henceforth
comply with this schedule in the matter of laying of the Orders issued
under various Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.
(131st Report)
(Presented on 15 December 2000)
“The Committee has, time and again, emphasized that it is essential
that in case there is a delay in the laying of Statutory Orders, the
concerned Ministry/Department should invariably append a delay
statement along with the notifications being laid so as to apprise
Parliament of the causes of delay. The Committee desires all Ministries/
Departments to take a note of this, since the intension is that through
the process of formulation of a delay statement the Ministry is able to
introspect, identify bottlenecks and devise remedial measures”.
(135th Report)
(Presented on 27 July 2001)

20
“In the opinion of the Committee, every notification should be
assigned a distinctive number in order to give it a separate identity and
similarly, no notification should be published/laid which does not carry a
notification number. The Committee expects all Ministries/Departments
of Government of India to exercise caution in this regard. In case where
there are more than one notifications under a single file, the Ministries/
Departments should ensure that the file number on each notification
should be suitably distinguished from one another.”
(152nd Report)
(Presented on 26 August 2004)
“In addition to the concern expressed by the Committee over delay
in laying of Notifications on the Table of the House, the Committee also
express their deep concern over delay in framing of rules/regulations
under different Acts. The Committee in its 47th report presented to the
House on 14.9.1981 has recommended that the rule-making process should
be completed within a period of six months of the coming into force on
an Act. The Committee has further recommended that in case a Ministry
is not able to adhere to this time limit, it should seek extension of time
for completing the rule-making process. The recommendation of the
committee reads as follows:-
“The Committee feels that the rule-making process could well have
been completed within the time limit of six months which the
Committee has laid down for making of rules under an Act after coming
into force of that Act. Where however, a Ministry does not find it possible
to adhere to the time limit, they should inform the Committee of the
reasons why they cannot make rules within the time limit and seek
extension of time for completing the rule-making process.”
The Committee is constrained to take note of the fact that the
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are not complying with
the Committee’s recommendation to complete the process of framing of

21
subordinate legislation contemplated under various Acts of Parliament
within a period of six months. At the same time, the Committee also
does not receive requests for extension of time for completing the rule-
making process in terms of its recommendations as above from most of
the Ministries/Departments. The Committee takes a serious note of the
prevailing situation in which the Ministries/Departments are neither
able to complete the task of framing rules/regulations under different
Acts within the given six months’ period nor do they suo-motu approach
the Committee for seeking extension of time. The Committee further
notes that in order to ensure timely framing of rules/regulations it has
taken an initiative to monitor the progress of framing of subordinate
legislation in respect of all legislations brought about by different
Ministries/Departments of Government of India from the year 2003
onwards with a view to ensure that the framing of subordinate legislation
is not delayed. The Committee, however, finds that the responses from
the Ministries/Departments have not been prompt in this monitoring
exercise undertaken on behalf of the Committee.
In view of the above position, the Committee once again reiterates
its recommendation that the Ministries/Departments should ensure
putting in place subordinate legislation positively within a period of six
months of coming into force of the Act. The Committee further
recommends that in case the Ministry fails to meet with this deadline,
they should invariably approach the Committee for seeking extension
of time. The Committee further recommends that in cases where the
time limit of six months is not adhered to, they should, while laying
rules/regulations before the Parliament invariably lay a statement
explaining the reasons why the framing of rules/regulations was delayed
beyond six months so as to keep the Parliament apprised of the compliance
of the Parliament’s mandate conferred upon the Executive.”
(192nd Report)
(Presented on 26 August 2011)

22
Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are laid by different Ministries
on the Table of the House under various provisions of parent Acts passed
by Parliament. These Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are published
in the official Gazette before being laid on the Table of the House. Even
after they are laid, it is very difficult to get access to these notifications.
The Committee recommends that such Rules/Regulations/Orders, etc.
laid on the Table of the House should be invariably uploaded on the
websites of respective Ministries immediately on the same day when
they have been laid on the Table of the House, for information of
Members of Parliament and people at large for their easy access.
201st Report
(Presented on 14th December, 2012)

INTRODUCTION
1. I, the Chairperson of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having
been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf, this Two
Hundred and Ninth Report of the Committee.
2. The Committee examined the matters that came up while scrutinizing
the Hallmarking Scheme and Certain Rules/Regulations framed u nder the
Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 and issues relating to them along with
the comments received from the concerned Governments.
3. The observations and recommendations of the Committee are contained
in the Report.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report in its meeting
held on the 27th August, 2013.
MAY A SINGH
Chairperson,
Committee on Subordinate Legislation
Rajya Sabha.
NEW DELHI;
3rd September, 2013
(iii)

1
Report on The Hallmarking Scheme and
Certain Rules/ Regulations framed under the
Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986
The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), an autonomous statutory
organization, came into existence after repealing of erstwhile Indian Standards
Institution (Certification Marks) Act, 1952, through an Act of Parliament i.e.
the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 dated 26th November 1986, on
1 April 1987. The new Act has, therefore, a broadened scope with more powers
taking over the staff, assets, liabilities and functions of erstwhile Indian
Standards Institution (ISI). Through this change over, Government envisaged
building a climate for quality culture and consciousness and greater participation
of consumers in formulation and implementation of national standards.
2. The Committee received a representation dated the 4th October, 2010
from the Forum for Good Governance, New Delhi regarding illegal operation
of Hallmarking Scheme for Gold Jewellery by the Bureau of Indian Standards
(BIS) and Department of Consumer Affairs in contravention of the BIS Act,
1986 as no regulations for governing the licences granted under the Scheme
have been laid down. A copy of the representation was forwarded to the Ministry
of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Department of Consumer
Affairs) for their comments/clarifications on the issues contained thereon on
the 31st December, 2010. The Ministry furnished their comments/clarifications
(Annexure-I) on the 14th January, 2011. The Committee thereafter held
discussions on the Hallmarking Scheme with the representatives of the Ministry
of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Department of Consumer
Affairs), Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Department of Industrial Policy
and Promotion), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and Minerals and Metals
Trading Corporation (MMTC) on the 19th January, 2011 in New Delhi and
again with the representatives of the MMTC, BIS, along with Assaying Centres
and the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Department

2
of Consumer Affairs) at Kumarakom on 23rd June, 2011. Study Notes on the
above discussions are placed at Annexure II and III. The Ministry’s comments
on the representation and the issues taken up for discussion during the above
said meetings are enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs.
3. The main issue for consideration of the Committee was that Gold Jewellery
Hallmarking Certification Scheme of BIS contravened the BIS Act as no
regulations for governing the licences granted under the Scheme had been laid
down, as required under Section 15 of the BIS Act. Secondly, in the absence
of regulations how and under which provisions of the BIS Act, 1986 or rules/
regulations, BIS had been operating the Hallmarking Scheme. The comments
of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Department
of Consumer Affairs) on the representation are given as under:-
“According to Section 2 (t) of the BIS Act, Standard Mark means the
Bureau of Indian Standards Certification Mark specified by BIS to
represent a particular Indian Standard. Rule 9 of the BIS Rules, 1987
provides that the Standard mark in relation to each Indian Standard shall
be published by the Bureau in the Official Gazette. Accordingly, the Bureau
notified the Standard Marks for IS 1417:1999 and ISI 2112-2003 in the
Gazette dated 27.04.2000 and 18.01.2006, respectively. Under the
Hallmarking Scheme for Gold and Silver Jewellery, licences are granted
to jewelers to enable them to get their jewellery certified for its fineness
in accordance with the requirements of ISI 1417:1999 ‘Gold and Gold
Alloys, Jewellery/ Artifacts-Fineness and Marking-Specification (Third
Revision)’ and ISI 2112:2003 ‘Silver and Silver Alloys, Jewellery/
Artifacts-Fineness and Marking-Specification’ and use the notified
standard mark on them. The provisions for grant of license to use the
Standard Mark in respect of any product against a particular standard
are contained in the Bureau of Indian Standards (Certification) Regulations,
1998. Gold and Silver jewellery are the products for which license can
be given”.

3
4. The Ministry further informed the Committee that the Scheme was
introduced in 2000 as a voluntary scheme. In order to make the Scheme
mandatory, Government has been considering an amendment to the BIS Act.
Further, the subject “BIS- Hallmarking of Jewellery” was selected by the
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Food, Consumer Affairs and Public
Distribution for examination in the year 2010. The Committee in its 9th Report
submitted to the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha on 31st August, 2010 strongly
recommended the Department to finalize the modalities of the Bill (for
amendment of the BIS Act) for its early introduction in Parliament so as to
bring the hallmarking under Mandatory Certification. The Committee also felt
that a lot more needed to be done to make the Scheme popular and make
people aware about the benefits of the Scheme and desired that BIS should
organize more publicity campaigns to educate the people at large about the
benefits of the scheme. The aim is that the common consumer gets gold and
silver jewellery of the purity declared by the jeweler. The Ministry was of the
considered view that no separate regulations were required as the existing BIS
Certification Regulations were adequate to cover voluntary hallmarking license
and that no difficulty or legal problems had been encountered so far.
Implementation of the Scheme was already being done as per these regulations.
5. Based on the Ministry’s comments, the issues that came up for discussion
during the Committee’s meetings held on 19th January, 2011 and 23rd June,
2011, included: (i) whether Ministry’s position that ‘no separate regulations
are required for hallmarking license’ was in contradiction with Section 15(1)
of the BIS Act, 1986 which provided that the Bureau may grant, renew, suspend
or cancel a license in such a manner as may be determined by regulations; and
Section 15(2) which provides that the grant or renewal of the license shall be
subject to such conditions and on payment of such fees as may be determined
by regulations; (ii) action taken pursuant to the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Food, Consumer Affairs and Public Distribution’s
recommendations for early introduction of amendment to the BIS Act so as to

4
bring hallmarking under mandatory certification; (iii) steps taken by Government
to make hallmarking Scheme more popular; (iv) the legal remedy available to
consumers who are cheated by the jewellers and whether BIS would be legally
empowered to take action against the delinquent jewellers; and (v) whether
BIS undertakes frequent inspection of assaying centres and steps taken by BIS
to prevent adulteration of gold.
6. The Committee was informed that Hallmarking Scheme for Gold Jewellery
was launched by BIS in April, 2000 to protect consumers against victimization
due to irregular gold quality, develop export competitiveness and make India as
a gold market centre in the world. The gold jewellery hallmarking licenses
were regulated by the Bureau of Indian Standards (Certifications) Regulations,
1988 and that most of the standards prescribed by the BIS were generally
voluntary and consensus based. Under the Scheme, a jeweller has to obtain
licence from BIS to get his jewellery hallmarked from a BIS recognized Assaying
and Hallmarking Centre. The Scheme thus does not grant self marking rights
to jewellers. The Hallmarking Centres are recognized by BIS based on laid
down criteria after ensuring that the Centre has required infrastructure for
assaying and hallmarking of gold jewellery, as well as adequate arrangement
for security and safety of articles.
7. Bureau of Indian Standards, under the administrative control of the
Department of Consumer Affairs has been operating the Gold Jewellery
Hallmarking Scheme. People purchased hallmarked jewellery under the belief
that hallmarking was legal and they would have legal remedies against the
dishonest jewellers. However, the Scheme did not have a legal backing and the
Hallmarking Scheme for Gold Jewellery was being allowed to run illegally in
total defiance to the provisions of section 15 of the BIS Act and without any
Regulations. The Ministry in their reply stated that the gold jewellery hallmarking
licenses were regulated by the Bureau of India Standards (Certifications)
Regulations, 1988 and that most of the standards prescribed by the BIS were

5
generally voluntary and consensus based. On the issue of quality maintenance
in ISI certified products, BIS informed that day-to-day checking was not done
given the spread and size of the country. However, inspection was done
periodically and the labs which gave ISI certifications had to fulfil the
requirements prescribed by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and
Calibration Laboratories (NABL). Adequate surveillance was being maintained
on operations of the assaying and hallmarking centres. Section 14 of the BIS
Act gave powers to the Central Government to make some of the standards
mandatory in public interest. These standards were mandatory keeping in view
public health and safety involved therein. Whenever any standard was made
mandatory then all the producers of that particular product had to compulsorily
take license from the BIS. As per the BIS Act, offences against use of ISI/
Hallmark without licence and nonconformity of gold with declared purity are
constituted under section 11 of the Act and punishment for the offences under
Section11 is prescribed under Section 33 of the BIS Act. The Committee,
however, observed that orders referring to mandatory standards are
issued by the concerned Ministry and not by the Bureau of Indian
Standards or Department of Consumer Affairs and that the Bureau of
Indian Standards Certification Regulations, 1988, in reality, only
regulated the licenses for use of ISI Mark. As the Hallmarking Scheme
was not governed by any Regulations, the Hallmarking licenses granted
by BIS had no legal force and their violations did not constitute offences
under Section 11 and, therefore, not punishable under Section 33 of the
Act.
8. The Committee is of the view that the Hallmarking Scheme of
Gold Jewellery should be made mandatory by making an amendment to
the BIS Act and Department of Consumer Affairs and BIS may be directed
to urgently make regulations under Section 15 and Section 38 of BIS
Act, 1986 for governing the Hallmark Licences. The Committee is
surprised and fails to understand why BIS/ Government is averse/ hostile

6
to framing of regulations for hallmarking licences and how in the absence
of any regulations, hallmarking licences are being granted under Section
15 of the BIS Act. The Committee observes that in view of Section 15(1)
and 15(2), existence of Regulations is mandatory for grant of licenses
under the Hallmarking Certification Scheme.
9. The Committee observed that although BIS had specified hall-
marking charges which licensed jewellers paid to the recognized Assaying
and Hall-Marking Centers, for getting gold jewellery articles tested and
hall-marked, yet, BIS had no role in deciding pricing of Hall-Marked
jewellery articles. The Committee was not satisfied with the work of BIS
in this regard and expressed concern regarding the higher cost involved
in hall-marking of goods/articles and pointed towards the difference in
market prices of goods with and without hall-marking. BIS Act requires
appropriate Regulations for operating Hallmarking Schemes in terms
of section 15 of the BIS Act, 1987. The Committee, accordingly, directs
the Ministry/BIS to take immediate/ necessary action in this regard.
10. The Committee recommends that assaying and hallmarking should
be made mandatory not only for the protection of the customer but also
for the viability of units established all over the country. Also, to provide
assurance of quality, hallmarking scheme may be made mandatory for
exporters of gold jewellery. Further, the licence to assaying and
hallmarking centres should be granted area-wise to avoid inter se
competition. In the Committee’s view, the Indian Hallmarking Council,
an independent body, under the BIS should be set up with Members of
Trade and Industry to monitor the operation of the scheme and enforce
regulations framed and notified by BIS/ Government.
11. The Committee observes that the registration scheme started by
Government in consultation with BIS is akin to granting/ distributing
licences to industries and sacrificing the interests of consumers as well

7
as the quality. In Committee’s view the registration scheme is killing
the existing revenue earning scheme i.e. the BIS Product Certification
Scheme popularly known as ISI Mark Scheme. This simplified procedure
for granting licences to the industry at the cost of the consumer will put
all checks and balances of normal procedure to a naught. Infact, this
simplified procedure violates the provisions of the BIS Act/ Rules/
Regulations. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that BIS take
immediate necessary action to correct the procedure so that it does not
put companies applying for licence under normal procedure to
disadvantage.
12. The Committee feels that more needs to be done to popularize the
scheme by creating awareness among the consumers and such awareness
campaigns should also highlight benefits which would accrue to the
jewellers through hallmarking. Further, in view of the capital intensive
nature of the project, BIS may explore the possibility of granting subsidy/
other incentive for all units established for promotion of the scheme.
13. The Committee also examined the BIS (Terms and Conditions of Service
of Employees) Regulations, 2007 and a questionnaire on the subject matter
was forwarded to the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public
Distribution (Department of Consumer Affairs) for their comments/clarifications
on the 14th January, 2011. The comments/clarifications of the Ministry on the
questionnaire are placed at Annexure-IV. The Committee also discussed the
subject matter with the Department of Consumer Affairs, Ministry of Consumer
Affairs, Food and Public Distribution and Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) at
its meeting held on the 19th January, 2011.
14. The Ministry informed the Committee that implementation of the Central
Pay Commission Recommendations (CPC) necessitated the framing of the
BIS (Terms and Conditions of Service of Employees) Regulations, 2007. The
Ministry further informed the Committee on the following issues, (i) As per
Regulation 17, BIS employees were entitled for medical facilities under Central

8
Government Health Scheme (CGHS). The employees not covered under the
CGHS were entitled to benefits as admissible to the employees of Central
Government Employees under Central Civil Services (Medical Attendance)
Rules, 1944 (CSMA). The present amount of monetary ceiling per annum was
over and above the benefits under CSMA Rules for reimbursement of medical
expenses including OPD charges. This was to facilitate treatment from any
registered medical practitioner; (ii) Revised pay scales as per the 6th Pay
Commission had been implemented in the BIS with the approval of the
Government. However, the first Schedule of the Regulations was yet to be
amended as certain discrepancies were observed in a few categories of Group
‘B’ Posts for which the matter had been taken up with the Government; (iii)
Consequent upon the upgradation of the erstwhile employees of Group ‘D’ to
Group ‘C’, the insurance cover as well as the contribution payable by the BIS
employees had been enhanced w.e.f. February, 2010. However, Sl. No. 6 of
the Second Schedule appended to the Regulations was yet to be amended as
the matter was under consideration with the Ministry; (iv) Promotion prospects
of BIS Scientific Cadre Officers were made in accordance with Government
of India’s Flexible Complementing Scheme (FCS) and duly incorporated in the
BIS (Recruitment to Scientific Cadre) Regulations, 2002; (v) BIS was short of
staff. The main difficulties before BIS in this regard were (a) non availability
of suitable candidates to fill the posts through direct recruitment, and (b) non
availability of candidates with the prescribed qualifications and experience in
BIS Laboratory Cadre for filing up the scientific cadre posts through promotion;
(vi) The 2007 Regulations provided for filling up of posts through promotion/
transfer on deputation/Direct Recruitment. BIS had made efforts to address
this problem by (a) reviving some posts that had been abolished, (b) advertising
the posts to be filled and (c) taking steps as per the provisions of the said
Regulations for filling up posts that had not been filled up yet.
15. The Committee, thereafter, enquired about (i) the reasons for not holding
any meeting of BIS since 28th July, 2003 in violation of Rule 5(2) of BIS

9
Rules, 1987; (ii) the reasons for outsourcing part of BIS’s work and whether
the same was mandated under the BIS Act and Rules; (iii) prospects of promotion
for scientific cadre officers working in BIS as compared to scientists working
in other Government undertakings, training facilities provided to employees of
BIS and other related issues. The Committee observed that (i) Shortage of
manpower in BIS, especially non-scientific officers which led to certain
essential items of work relating to legal, Human Resource Department,
Administration, etc. being attended to by some scientific officers in
addition to their normal duties; (ii) BIS had not held any meetings since
28th July, 2003 in violation of Rule 5(2) of the BIS Rules, 1987, which
mandates that the Bureau shall meet twice in a year; and (iii) Section
10(1)(l) of BIS Act, 1986 empowered BIS to appoint agents in India or
abroad for inspection, testing and such other purposes as may be
prescribed. Based on this provision, BIS had outsourced its work relating
to routine surveillance visits after the grant of licence. The Committee
wondered to what extent this was justified.
16. Director General, BIS informed the Committee that there was shortage
of staff in BIS especially in the scientific cadre as the Interview Board could
not find suitable candidates. The problem was compounded by the standing
orders of the Department of Personnel and Training (DOPT) which stated that
if a post is lying vacant for more than one year, it stands abolished. Regarding
training of employees, DG , BIS stated that the National Institute of Training
for Standardization (NITS) Noida, a training Institute under the Bureau conducts
training on a wide range of subjects for staff and officers of BIS for capacity
building and also organizes international training programmes for developing
countries as well. The Committee could not fathom why BIS could not get
requisite number of suitable candidates for scientific cadre when other
organizations were getting the requisite number of such candidates.
17. Further, during the course of examination of the Electrical Wires, Cables,
Appliances and Protection Devices and Accessories (Quality Control) Order,

10
2003, on which the Committee presented a Report to the House on the 3rd
May, 2013, the Committee held meetings with the representatives of the Ministry
of Commerce and Industry (Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion),
Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Department of
Consumer Affairs) and Bureau of Indian Standards. During the course of the
discussions, the Committee raised certain points regarding the administrative
setup and functioning of the Bureau of Indian Standards and functioning under
the administrative control of the Government through the Department of
Consumer Affairs, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution.
The points that came up for discussion with the Ministry of Consumer Affairs,
Food and Public Distribution (Department of Consumer Affairs) thereon are
given in the succeeding paragraphs.
18. Although BIS had specified hall-marking charges which licensed jewellers
paid to the recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, for getting gold
jewellery articles tested and hallmarked yet BIS had no role in deciding pricing
of Hallmarked jewellery articles. The Committee was not satisfied with the
work of BIS in this regard and expressed concern regarding the higher
cost involved in hallmarking of goods/articles and pointed towards the
difference in market prices of goods with and without hallmarking.
19. As per the BIS Act, 1987, the Director General of BIS is to be appointed
by the Central Government as per the BIS (Appointment, Terms and Conditions
of Service of Director General) Rules, 1987. These rules lay down the norms,
qualifications and the procedure for appointment of Director General of BIS.
The Committee expressed serious concern on observing that generalist
officers, especially from All India Services, were being appointed as
Director General (DG) and Additional Director Generals (ADGs) of BIS
when the BIS Rules (Appointment, Terms and Conditions of Service of
Director General), 1987 had specifically prescribed technical qualifications
for the posts of DG and ADGs. However, BIS Rules had been totally by-
passed while appointing DG, BIS on deputation. Firstly, there was no provision

11
in BIS Rules for appointment of DG , BIS on deputation basis. The Committee
had shown its displeasure over the failure of BIS to find any suitable candidate
from technical background when the post of Director General lied vacant
repeatedly in 2004, 2006 and 2008. The Selection Committee was, therefore,
compelled to approach the Department of Personnel and Training so that they
nominate an officer empanelled as Additional Secretary with technical/scientific
degree for that post. The Committee observed that BIS being a specialized
agency and when the BIS (Appointment, Terms and Conditions of Service
of Director General) Rules, 1987 particularly provided for technical
qualification for the post of Director-General, appointment of generalist
officers was tantamount to violation of recruitment rules in BIS. The
Committee took note of the fact that later on the Cabinet Secretariat separately
advised the Department to review and revise the Recruitment Rules. The draft
Rules prescribing revised eligibility conditions for the post of Director General
were then submitted to Cabinet Secretariat and DOP&T for concurrence/
approval which had been received from DOPT. Moreover, it seems that BIS
did not heed to the advice of the Cabinet Committee on Appointments (CCA)
and without amending the Recruitment Rules, sought its approval for
appointment of DG, BIS on deputation again in July, 2008 when a vacancy of
DG arose due to promotion of erstwhile DG , BIS in May, 2008.
20. Bureau of India Standards is a scientific organization and has a Flexible
Complementing Scheme (FCS) for promotions of its scientific officers, which
leaves much scope for violating the provisions of FCS and DOPT Circular for
promoting officers without giving regard to eligibility criteria. It is alleged that
BIS is making mockery of Flexible Complimenting Scheme (FCS) for promotion
of BIS Scientific Cadre in violation of BIS Regulations and DOPT instructions.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends that specific/relevant rules
should be in place to ensure that the existing systems do not make
mockery of Flexible Complimenting Scheme (FCS) for promotion of BIS
Scientific Cadre Officers in violation of BIS Regulations and DOPT
instructions.

12
21. While BIS Act under Section 10(1)(l) has a provision for appointing
agents/outsourcing jobs for carrying out inspections under BIS Product
Certification Scheme, but in the process of appointing agents BIS has violated
many provisions of its Principal Act, Rules, Regulations and also its own
Certification Manual. Thus, procedure given in BIS rules has not been followed.
The Committee observed that BIS had been outsourcing part of its work
and expressed concern whether this was mandated under the BIS Acts
and Rules and how BIS ensured that these outsourced agencies appoint
qualified and technically competent staff.
22. On the issue of the working of BIS and ‘Certification Work’, the
Committee further wanted to know the reason for outsourcing the certification
work to private agencies which was earlier being done by BIS. The Committee
also inquired about the standards or qualifications prescribed for the private
agencies and whether BIS undertook quality audit of working of these agencies.
The Committee thus questioned about the violation of the rules in this regard.
The Ministry informed the Committee that due to increase in work load and
shortage of officers in the BIS, the work relating to routine surveillance visits
after the grant of license was outsourced. The work relating to preliminary
inspection for grant of license and other statutory functions including
certification were, however, discharged by BIS officers only. As per Section
10 (1) (l) of BIS Act, 1986, agents can be appointed in India or abroad, for
inspection testing and such other purposes as may be prescribed. The
laboratories of the agents are then counter-checked by the BIS personnel to
find out whether they have required facilities for testing and whether laboratories
are certified by National Accreditation Board for Laboratories (NABL). One of
the technical requirements at the time of tendering for engagement as authorized
agencies is that the people deployed for inspection work of BIS should have
Degree in Engineering/Post Graduate Degree in Science. The BIS Committee
which selects these agents ensures that these agents fulfil the technical
requirements as envisaged in the BIS Act. The inspection reports submitted by
outsourced agencies are then scrutinized by BIS officers and discrepancies, if

13
any found, are conveyed to the agencies for necessary actions at their end.
BIS officers also undertook quality audit of these units. The Committee
observed that agencies usually employed diploma holders or ITI trained
people for inspecting companies and their products while in the BIS Act
it was provided that only scientific cadre officers should inspect the
companies.
23. The Committee observes that though the BIS Act provided for
appointment of Advisory Committee, the Rules framed in this regard
did not provide for the qualifications, experience etc. of the Members to
be appointed to these Advisory Committees. In the view of the
Committee, the Rules of BIS should have been made more specific and,
accordingly, advises the Ministry to initiate immediate/necessary action
in this regard. The Ministry in its reply stated that Section 5 of the Bureau of
Indian Standard Act, 1986 provided for number of Advisory Committees each
consisting of a Chairman and such other members as may be determined by
Regulations. “Member” as per BIS Act meant any member of the Bureau and
could represent Government, Industry, Scientific and Research Institutions,
and other interests.
24. Further after studying the rules/regulations framed by BIS so far,
the Committee was of the view that there was an absence of proper
delegation of powers at different levels and therefore inquired about the
action that had been initiated by the Ministry/BIS to amend the BIS
Rules in this regard. The Ministry in turn informed the Committee that under
Regulation 3 of the BIS (Powers and Duties of Director General) Regulations,
1987 on account of administrative efficiency, Director General may delegate
any of his powers or duties as prescribed in the Regulations to any officers not
below the rank of Deputy Director of the Bureau. Accordingly, Director General
had appropriately delegated various powers to the subordinate officers of the
BIS. Further with the view to increase efficiency, Bureau itself had delegated
its powers for grant of license to the Heads of various Branch Offices of the
BIS.

14
25. The Committee also raised concern about the inadequate manpower
of BIS and took note of the fact that officers were holding multiple posts
for which different qualifications and experience were needed. The
Committee viewed it seriously as this kind of situation would certainly
hamper the functional efficacy of any organization. However, the
Committee was informed that BIS at that particular time had 411 scientific
officers and 34 non scientific officers against the strength of 579 and 57
respectively indicated in the relevant Regulations. Due to shortage of non
scientific officers, certain essential items of work relating to Legal, Human
Resource Department, Administration, etc. were being attended to by some of
the scientific officers in addition to their normal duties so that the functioning
of BIS was not hampered and this arrangement was done in the interest of the
organization. The Ministry further informed that the Consumer Affairs
Department of BIS was a part of technical support service to be handled by
scientific cadre officers as the activity required knowledge of standardization.
Officers of that Department also handled the functions of standards promotion,
educational utilization of standard programmes, standard formulation, etc, which
were of scientific nature. However, in the Committee’s opinion, the core
functions of BIS should not be outsourced to private agencies as they
have no accountability to the Parliament. Moreover, the Committee
observes that the BIS Act needs to be suitably amended to allow BIS to
impose stringent penalties and punishments to the defaulters of BIS
Standards.
26. The Committee also observed that BIS Rules regarding appeals
had been violated. There are instances of appeals being heard and decided by
the Executive Committee of the BIS ( the Appellate Authority in BIS) where
Director General was present as a member, who himself has passed orders
against which appeals are being heard. This is in violation of CCS (CCA)
Rules, 1965 and also against the Principle of Natural Justice.

15
GENERAL OBSERV ATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE
COMMITTEE
27. The Committee is of the view that the Hallmarking Scheme of
Gold Jewellery should be made mandatory by making an amendment to
the BIS Act and Department of Consumer Affairs and BIS may be directed
to urgently make regulations under Section 15 and Section 38 of BIS
Act, 1986 for governing the Hallmark Licences. The Committee observes
that in view of Section 15(1) and 15(2), existence of Regulations is
mandatory for grant of licenses under the Hallmarking Certification
Scheme.
28. The Committee observed that although BIS had specified hall-
marking charges which licensed jewellers paid to the recognized Assaying
and Hallmarking Centers, for getting gold jewellery articles tested and
hallmarked, yet, BIS had no role in deciding pricing of Hallmarked
jewellry articles. The Committee was not satisfied with the work of BIS
in this regard and expressed concern regarding the higher cost involved
in hallmarking of goods/articles and pointed towards the difference in
market prices of goods with and without hallmarking. BIS Act requires
appropriate Regulations for operating Hallmarking Schemes in terms
of section 15 of the BIS Act, 1987. The Committee, accordingly, directs
the Ministry/BIS to take immediate/necessary action in this regard.
29. The Committee expressed serious concern on observing that
generalist officers, especially from All India Services, are being appointed
as Director General (DG) and Additional Director Generals (ADGs) of
BIS when the BIS Rules (Appointment, Terms and Conditions of Service
of Director General), 1987 had specifically prescribed technical
qualifications for the posts of DG and ADGs. The Committee, therefore,
impresses upon the Department of Consumer Affairs not to violate the
BIS (Appointment, Terms and Conditions of Service of Director General)
Rules, 1987 while appointing DG or ADGs in the BIS.

16
30. The Committee is concerned about the acute shortage of manpower
in BIS and took note of the fact that officers were holding multiple posts
for which different qualifications and experience were needed. The
Committee viewed it seriously as this kind of situation would  certainly
hamper the functional efficacy of any organization. In the Committee’s
opinion, the core functions of BIS should not be outsourced to private
agencies as they have no accountability to the Parliament. Moreover,
the Committee observes that the BIS Act needs to be suitably amended
to allow BIS to impose stringent penalties and punishments to the
defaulters of BIS Standards.
31. The Committee observed that BIS had outsourced the work relating
to routine surveillance visits after the grant of licence due to shortage
of staff and officers. The Committee, therefore, reiterates the need to
strengthen the staff of BIS, to increase the number of BIS labs so as to
reduce imbalances in the country in respect of distribution of BIS
laboratories. Moreover, the Committee feels that the core functions of
BIS should not be outsourced as private agencies have no accountability
to the Parliament.
32. BIS is a scientific organization and has a Flexible Complementing
Scheme (FCS) for promotions of its scientific officers. The Committee,
accordingly, recommends that specific rules should be framed to ensure
that the existing Flexible Complimenting Scheme (FCS) for promotion
of BIS Scientific Cadre Officers does not work in violation of BIS
Regulations and DOPT Circulars. The Committee is also of the opinion
that there should be proper delegation of powers at different levels in
the organization so that BIS can perform its work without any hindrance.
33. The Committee observes that though the BIS Act provides for
appointment of Advisory Committee, the Rules framed in this regard
do not provide for the qualifications, experience etc. of the Members
to be appointed to these Advisory Committees. In the view of the

17
Committee, the Rules of BIS should have been made more specific
and, accordingly, advises the Ministry to initiate immediate/ necessary
action in this regard .
34. The Committee feels that Department of Consumer Affairs and
BIS need to do a lot more to arouse mass awareness about the benefits
of the Hallmarking Scheme through publicity campaigns in electronic
and print media.
35. In the Committee’s view, the Department of Consumer Affairs, as
the administrative Ministry for enforcement of the BIS Act and BIS,
has both authority and responsibility to regulate BIS and ensure that
the affairs of BIS are conducted in accordance with the BIS Act.

(a) The relevant Indian Standards relating to the BIS Hallmarking Scheme

(1) IS 417 : 1999 'Gold and Gold Alloys, Jewellery/Artefacts -

Indian Standard shall be published by the Bureau in the Official
21

22
Gazette. Accordingly, the Bureau notified the Standard Marks for
IS 1417:1999 and IS 2112-2003 in the Gazette on 27-04-2000 and

to get their jewellery certified for its fineness in accordance with
the requirements of IS 1417:1999 'Gold and Gold Alloys, Jewellery/

and IS 2112: 2003 'Silver and Silver Alloys: Jewellery/ Artefacts-

mark in respect of any product against a particular standard are
contained in the Bureau of Indian Standards (Certification)
Regulations, 1988. Gold and Silver Jewellery are also the products,
for which, license can be given.
(c) The Scheme was introduced in the year 2000 as a voluntary
Scheme. In order to make the Scheme mandatory the Government
has been considering an amendment to the BIS Act. It is expected
that this Bill will be introduced in the Parliament this year.
(d) The subject “BIS Hallmarking of Jewellery" was selected by
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Food, Consumer Affairs and
Public Distribution for examination during the year 2010. The
Committee held discussions with the representatives of Consumer

2010, 22 May, 2010, 1st July, 2010 and 21st July, 2010. The
Committee in its 9th Report submitted to Lok Sabha and Rajya
Sabha on 31st August, 2010 strongly recommended to the
Department to take up the matter with utmost seriousness and finalize
the modalities of the Bill (for amendment of the BIS Act) for its
early introduction in the Parliament so as, to bring the hallmarking
under Mandatory Certification. The Committee also felt that a lot

23
more needs to be done to make the Scheme popular and make
people aware about the benefits of the Scheme and desired that BIS
should organize more publicity campaigns to educate the people at
large about the benefits of the Scheme. The aim is that common

representatives of the Department of Consumer Affairs, Director General, Bureau
of Indian Standards (BIS), representatives of Department of Industrial Policy
and Promotion and representatives of MMTC. The Chairman, in his opening

26
remarks; enquired about the shortage of manpower in BIS and the steps taken

1987; the reasons for outsourcing part of BIS's work and whether the same
